theme: Why do the nations rage?, the anointed Son
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 2. This is the second psalm of the Psalter, and one of the most important messianic psalms. Read it as a drama with four voices: the nations, the LORD, the king, and the psalmist.
settingTheScene: Psalm 2 is a royal psalm, probably used at the coronation of a king in Jerusalem. It begins with nations in rebellion, moves to God’s answer from heaven, and ends with a call to submit. Along with Psalm 1, it forms the introduction to the Psalter. Psalm 1 is about the righteous person, and Psalm 2 is about the righteous king. Placed here, at the start of the books of Samuel, it points ahead to the king God will establish.
observation: “Why do the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain?” (v. 1).
“The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the LORD and against his anointed” (v. 2).
“Let us burst their bonds apart and cast away their cords from us” (v. 3).
“He who sits in the heavens laughs; the Lord holds them in derision” (v. 4).
“As for me, I have set my King on Zion, my holy hill” (v. 6).
“You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (v. 7).
“Ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage, and the ends of the earth your possession” (v. 8).
“Kiss the Son, lest he be angry… Blessed are all who take refuge in him” (vv. 12).
interpretation:
The psalm opens with a question that exposes the folly of human rebellion: “Why do the nations rage?” The kings of the earth gather against the LORD and his anointed, saying, “Let us burst their bonds apart.” They see God’s rule as a prison. But their plotting is “in vain.” It is the oldest delusion: that we can throw off the rule of our Creator and be free.

God’s response is striking. He laughs. It is not the laughter of cruelty. It is the laughter of one who is secure. The nations’ rage cannot touch him. He sits in heaven, and then he speaks, and his word is terrifying: “I have set my King on Zion.” God’s answer to rebellion is a king.

In verse 7, the king speaks. “You are my Son; today I have begotten you.” In ancient Israel, the king was called God’s son at his enthronement, a way of saying that he ruled as God’s representative. The promise to David in 2 Samuel 7:14 is in view, and you will read it soon. But the words reach beyond any ordinary king. The ends of the earth are promised to this Son, and “you shall break them with a rod of iron.”

The psalm ends with an invitation. The kings are told to be wise, to serve the LORD with fear, to kiss the Son, to submit. The final line is a beatitude: “Blessed are all who take refuge in him.” It echoes the “blessed” of Psalm 1:1. The Psalter begins and ends the introduction with blessing.

For Israel, the king in Jerusalem was a sign. But as Israel’s kings failed one after another, the psalm began to be read as a promise of a king still to come, the Messiah, who would truly rule the nations.
connection: The New Testament quotes Psalm 2 more than any other psalm. At Jesus’ baptism and transfiguration, the Father says, “You are my beloved Son” (Mark 1:11; 9:7). Acts 4:25-28 applies verses 1 and 2 to the plot against Jesus. Paul quotes verse 7 about the resurrection (Acts 13:33). Hebrews 1:5 and 5:5 use it of Christ’s sonship and priesthood. Revelation 2:27, 12:5, and 19:15 apply the rod of iron to his final victory.
application:
Ask whether you ever see God’s rule as a prison. Bring that to him honestly.

Take refuge in the Son. Name one fear, and place it in his hands.

Pray for leaders in your nation and for a spirit of humility among them.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what you do when the nations rage and plots seem to prosper.
Take refuge in the Son, and tell him so.
Ask him to teach you to rejoice with trembling.
